title: AI Video Hook Writer: 40 Hooks That Give Short Videos a Stronger First Line

# AI Video Hook Writer: 40 Hooks That Give Short Videos a Stronger First Line

At 0:01, a viewer’s thumb is already moving. If your opening sounds like a topic label—“Today I’m talking about productivity”—the video has asked for patience before it has created a reason to stay.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

An AI video hook writer helps turn a subject into an opening someone can understand instantly: a spoken first line, matching on-screen text, and a direction for the next beat. This page gives you 40 ready-to-adapt hooks, plus a simple way to choose and test one.

## Hooks for fitness videos

1. **Contrarian:** “Stop going to the gym every day.” On-screen: “Day 1 is where you quit.”
2. **Mistake:** “You’re not lazy. You’re doing week one wrong.” On-screen: “The week-one mistake.”
3. **Question:** “Why does motivation disappear after three workouts?” On-screen: “It’s not motivation.”
4. **Specific problem:** “This is why your workout plan dies on Thursday.” On-screen: “The Thursday drop-off.”
5. **Before/after setup:** “I stopped making this one gym promise to myself.” On-screen: “The promise that backfires.”

## Hooks for creator and social-media videos

6. **Pattern interrupt:** “Your video does not need a better camera first.” On-screen: “Fix this before gear.”
7. **Mistake:** “Most hooks fail before the speaker finishes the first sentence.” On-screen: “The opening mistake.”
8. **Challenge:** “Can you explain your video in seven words?” On-screen: “Try this test.”
9. **Contrarian:** “Stop introducing yourself at the start of every video.” On-screen: “Your name can wait.”
10. **Reveal:** “The boring part of your script is probably the first line.” On-screen: “Find the drag.”

## Hooks for small-business videos

11. **Customer question:** “Before you buy this, ask this one question.” On-screen: “Ask before buying.”
12. **Pain point:** “If customers keep asking the price, your offer may be unclear.” On-screen: “Why they only ask price.”
13. **Behind the scenes:** “Here’s the part of this order customers never see.” On-screen: “Behind this order.”
14. **Myth:** “More choices do not always make a customer more likely to buy.” On-screen: “Too many options?”
15. **Process:** “This is the first thing I check before sending an order.” On-screen: “Before it ships.”

## Hooks for money and career videos

16. **Question:** “What would change if you tracked one number for 30 days?” On-screen: “One number. 30 days.”
17. **Mistake:** “A raise conversation can go wrong before you mention a salary.” On-screen: “Don’t open like this.”
18. **Contrarian:** “Your budget does not need more categories.” On-screen: “It needs this instead.”
19. **Career tension:** “Being busy is not the same as being visible at work.” On-screen: “Busy vs. visible.”
20. **Practical promise:** “Use this sentence when you need to ask for more time.” On-screen: “Ask for time clearly.”

## Hooks for productivity and study videos

21. **Observation:** “Your to-do list may be making tomorrow harder.” On-screen: “The list problem.”
22. **Question:** “What do you do when a task takes five minutes but waits five days?” On-screen: “Why small tasks wait.”
23. **Mistake:** “Do not start studying by opening every tab.” On-screen: “Close these tabs.”
24. **Experiment:** “I tried planning only the next hour.” On-screen: “One-hour planning.”
25. **Reframe:** “Procrastination is sometimes a vague next step.” On-screen: “Make the next step smaller.”

## Hooks for food, beauty, and lifestyle videos

26. **Expectation reset:** “This recipe starts with the step most people skip.” On-screen: “Don’t skip this.”
27. **Taste test:** “I made this three ways so you do not have to.” On-screen: “Which version wins?”
28. **Problem-solution:** “If your makeup separates by lunch, check this first.” On-screen: “Why it separates.”
29. **Small change:** “This is the five-minute reset that makes my kitchen usable again.” On-screen: “Five-minute kitchen reset.”
30. **Honest comparison:** “The cheaper option surprised me for one reason.” On-screen: “The difference I noticed.”

## Hooks for education and explainer videos

31. **Plain-language opening:** “Here is the part nobody explains about [TOPIC].” On-screen: “The missing part.”
32. **Misconception:** “You probably learned this backwards.” On-screen: “Let’s fix it.”
33. **Question:** “Why does this simple rule have so many exceptions?” On-screen: “The exception problem.”
34. **Visual promise:** “Watch what happens when we change just one variable.” On-screen: “Change one thing.”
35. **Shortcut with a limit:** “This shortcut works—until this point.” On-screen: “Where it breaks.”

## Hooks for personal-story videos

36. **Moment of change:** “I knew this plan was not working when [MOMENT].” On-screen: “That was the signal.”
37. **Unexpected lesson:** “The advice I ignored was the advice I needed.” On-screen: “I got this wrong.”
38. **Tension:** “I almost quit because of a problem I had misunderstood.” On-screen: “The real problem.”
39. **Decision:** “I changed one rule, and it changed how I approached [TOPIC].” On-screen: “One rule changed it.”
40. **Reader bridge:** “If you keep restarting, this may sound familiar.” On-screen: “For the restarters.”

## How to pick a hook

Choose the hook based on what the viewer already feels, not the topic you want to cover.

- Use a **mistake** hook when the viewer is trying and getting a frustrating result.
- Use a **question** hook when the video answers a question they may already be asking.
- Use a **contrarian** hook when you can challenge familiar advice, then explain the limit honestly.
- Use a **specific-problem** hook when the viewer can recognize a precise moment of failure.
- Use a **story** hook when the lesson only makes sense after a real turning point.

A good first line creates a clear next question. It should not try to explain the whole video. If the opening says “Stop going to the gym every day,” the next beat needs to explain who that advice is for and why—not jump to an unrelated list.

## How to test a hook before filming

Write three versions for the same video: one question, one mistake, and one contrarian angle. Read each aloud once. Keep the one that is easiest to say without adding setup words.

Then check four things:

- Can a viewer understand the situation with the sound off from the on-screen text?
- Does the spoken line name a tension, question, or consequence?
- Does the next sentence answer the curiosity the hook creates?
- Does the hook fit the actual video, rather than making a promise the rest cannot support?

Keep a small record of what you tested: topic, hook type, spoken line, on-screen text, and what you would change next time. That turns “I need a better hook” into a repeatable editing decision.

## FAQ

### What does an AI video hook writer make?

It can help shape a topic into multiple hook options, with spoken wording, on-screen text, an angle, and supporting script direction.

### Should every hook be controversial?

No. Contrarian hooks can earn attention when the video can support the claim. A clear question or a specific mistake is often a better fit for practical, educational, or trust-based content.

### How long should the first spoken line be?

Make it short enough to say naturally before the video moves to its explanation. Remove greetings, broad labels, and context the viewer can infer from the screen.

### Can I use the same hook format repeatedly?

Yes, but vary the underlying tension. Repeating a format is useful when it helps viewers recognize your style; repeating the same vague promise is not.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the input and the shortened output:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
